# Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam

Journal: TOCECCS: Applied computing E-learningCCS: Computing
methodologies Natural language processingCCS: Computing
methodologies Computer vision

Nabor C. Mendonça
[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2972-9423 "ORCID 0000-0002-2972-9423")
email: <nabor@unifor.br> Affiliation: Post-Graduate Program in Applied
Informatics, University of Fortaleza, Av. Washington Soares, 1321, Edson
Queiroz, Fortaleza, Ceará, Brazil, 60811-905

###### Abstract.

The recent integration of visual capabilities into Large Language Models
(LLMs) has the potential to play a pivotal role in science and
technology education, where visual elements such as diagrams, charts,
and tables are commonly used to improve the learning experience. This
study investigates the performance of ChatGPT-4 Vision, OpenAI’s most
advanced visual model at the time the study was conducted, on the
Bachelor in Computer Science section of Brazil’s 2021 National
Undergraduate Exam (ENADE). By presenting the model with the exam’s open
and multiple-choice questions in their original image format and
allowing for reassessment in response to differing answer keys, we were
able to evaluate the model’s reasoning and self-reflecting capabilities
in a large-scale academic assessment involving textual and visual
content. ChatGPT-4 Vision significantly outperformed the average exam
participant, positioning itself within the top 10 best score percentile.
While it excelled in questions that incorporated visual elements, it
also encountered challenges with question interpretation, logical
reasoning, and visual acuity. A positive correlation between the model’s
performance in multiple-choice questions and the performance
distribution of the human participants suggests multimodal LLMs can
provide a useful tool for question testing and refinement. However, the
involvement of an independent expert panel to review cases of
disagreement between the model and the answer key revealed some poorly
constructed questions containing vague or ambiguous statements, calling
attention to the critical need for improved question design in future
exams. Our findings suggest that while ChatGPT-4 Vision shows promise in
multimodal academic evaluations, human oversight remains crucial for
verifying the model’s accuracy and ensuring the fairness of high-stakes
educational exams. The paper’s research materials are publicly available
at
[https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021).

###### Keywords: 

Multimodal Generative AI, ChatGPT-4 Vision, Educational Assessment,
Computer Science Education

## 1. Introduction

The advent of large language models (LLMs), such as OpenAI’s
ChatGPT ([OpenAI, 2023a](#bib.bib30)) and Google’s Gemini ([Google,
2023](#bib.bib13)), has ushered in a new era in natural language
processing. These models exhibit human-like performance in tasks
requiring complex reasoning, including abstract thinking,
problem-solving across diverse knowledge domains, coding, and
comprehending human emotions and motives ([Zhao et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib51); [Bubeck et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)). The recent
integration of visual capabilities into these models ([OpenAI,
2023b](#bib.bib31)) has the potential to play a pivotal role in
advancing their use in educational settings, particularly in the science
and technology fields, where visual elements such as diagrams, charts,
and tables are commonly used to offer a more comprehensive and engaging
learning experience ([Evagorou et al., 2015](#bib.bib10)).

Using LLMs like ChatGPT and Gemini in education presents novel
opportunities and challenges for students, educators, and standardized
exam creators ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib21); [Kasneci et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19)). These models offer students innovative tools for
exam preparation, potentially reshaping study habits and learning
methodologies ([Dai et al., 2023](#bib.bib8)). For educators, LLMs serve
as a resource to enrich teaching strategies and help tailor exam content
to better suit learning outcomes ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib52)).
Meanwhile, standardized exam creators could utilize these AI tools to
refine their questions, ensuring clarity, fairness, and appropriate
difficulty levels. However, the use of these models also introduces
concerns around accuracy, reliability, and potential for misuse,
highlighting the need for careful evaluation of visual LLMs in academic
settings ([Meyer et al., 2023](#bib.bib27); [Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib52)).

This study evaluates the accuracy of ChatGPT-4 Vision ([OpenAI,
2023c](#bib.bib32)), OpenAI’s most advanced visual model at the time the
study was conducted, in answering the Bachelor in Computer Science (BCS)
section of Brazil’s 2021 National Undergraduate Exam (ENADE) ([Inep,
2023](#bib.bib15)). Unlike most prior evaluations of ChatGPT and other
LLMs in academic assessments in Computer Science (e.g., ([Joshi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib18); [Richards et al., 2024](#bib.bib38); [Jalil et al.,
2023](#bib.bib16); [Bordt and von Luxburg, 2023](#bib.bib5))) and other
fields (e.g., ([Nori et al., 2023](#bib.bib28); [Frenkel and Emara,
2023](#bib.bib11); [Pursnani et al., 2023](#bib.bib35))), we presented
all ENADE BCS exam questions to ChatGPT-4 Vision in their original image
formats as seen by human participants. This method allowed a
comprehensive evaluation of the model’s multimodal reasoning abilities,
challenging its linguistic and visual interpretation capabilities in a
particular education domain.

Additionally, we explored the model’s capacity for self-reflection by
prompting it to reassess its initial responses when presented with
differing answer keys. When ChatGPT-4 Vision’s answers diverged from the
answer keys after reassessment, we assembled an independent panel of
computer science researchers from various Brazilian universities to
evaluate the accuracy of the model’s responses. This additional layer of
expert review provided insights into the model’s reasoning accuracy and
the exam questions’ quality regarding clarity and objectivity.

We further correlated the model’s performance with the difficulty and
discrimination levels of the multiple-choice questions, as reported by
ENADE organizers. This analysis aimed to provide insights into how the
model’s proficiency compared to that of the human participants, offering
a more nuanced understanding of the model’s capabilities and limitations
in a real-world academic assessment context.

Our study aims to answer the following quantitative research questions:

RQ1::  
How well does ChatGPT-4 Vision perform in answering ENADE 2021 BCS open
questions?

RQ2::  
How well does ChatGPT-4 Vision perform in answering ENADE 2021 BCS
multiple-choice questions?

RQ3::  
How often did ChatGPT-4 change or maintain its response when confronted
with a disagreeing official answer?

RQ4::  
What is ChatGPT-4 Vision’s ENADE 2021 BCS exam final score, and how does
it compare with the exam participants?

In addition, we examined the reasoning, accuracy, and reflective
analysis of ChatGPT-4 Vision, and the independent expert assessments to
answer the following qualitative research question:

RQ5::  
What are the main challenges ChatGPT-4 Vision faced in answering ENADE
2021 BCS open and multiple-choice questions?

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- •
  We have evaluated ChatGPT-4 Vision’s multimodal reasoning abilities on
  the ENADE 2021 BCS exam, a large-scale computer science academic
  assessment test involving textual and visual content, providing all
  questions in image format.
- •
  We have explored ChatGPT-4 Vision’s capacity for self-reflection by
  allowing it to reassess its initial responses when confronted with
  differing answer keys.
- •
  We have correlated ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance with the difficulty
  and discrimination levels of the exam’s multiple-choice questions,
  offering insights into how the model’s proficiency compares to that of
  the human participants.
- •
  We have involved an independent panel of computer science researchers
  from various Brazilian universities to evaluate the accuracy of
  ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses that conflicted with the official answer,
  providing further insights into the model’s limitations and the exam
  questions’ design quality.

Overall, our results reveal ChatGPT-4 Vision’s impressive yet limited
performance in reasoning about multimodal content in computer science
academic assessments. In particular, ChatGPT-4 Vision significantly
outperformed the average exam participant, achieving the top 10 best
score percentile. However, the model faced several challenges with
question interpretation, logical reasoning, and visual acuity. These
findings underscore the continued need for human oversight in verifying
LLMs’s accuracy in solving complex reasoning tasks. Moreover, some
disagreements between the model, the expert panel, and the official
answer raise concerns about the quality of some exam questions. Given
the significant impact of ENADE on Brazil’s undergraduate academic
rankings, our findings call attention to the critical need for improved
question design and quality control in future ENADE exams to ensure a
fair educational assessment process.

To facilitate the replication and extension of our study, we have made
our research materials publicly available at
[https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021).
This repository contains the exam questions, response standards, answer
keys, ChatGPT-4’s full conversations, and experts’ evaluations, in
Portuguese and English.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Section [2](#S2 "2. Related Work ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
discusses related work in LLM evaluations in logical reasoning tasks and
educational assessments in computer science and other domains.
Section [3](#S3 "3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
provides background information on ENADE and the 2021 BCS exam.
Section [4](#S4 "4. Study Method ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")

Section [5](#S5 "5. Results ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
presents the results of our study, and
Section [6](#S6 "6. Discussion ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")

Section [7](#S7 "7. Conclusion ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")

## 2. Related Work

Our work touches on several areas of related research, including LLM
evaluations in general logical reasoning tasks ([Bubeck et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib22); [Mao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25); [Espejel et al., 2023](#bib.bib9)), using LLMs in
educational assessments in computer science ([Joshi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17); [Richards et al., 2024](#bib.bib38); [Jalil et al.,
2023](#bib.bib16); [Bordt and von Luxburg, 2023](#bib.bib5); [Mahon
et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)) and other domains ([Nori et al.,
2023](#bib.bib28); [Toyama et al., 2023](#bib.bib40); [Frenkel and
Emara, 2023](#bib.bib11); [Pursnani et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)), and
recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ([Zhang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib49); [Mayne, 2024](#bib.bib26); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44); [Zhang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib48)). Also of interest
are related works that evaluated LLMs’ effectiveness in answering
Brazil’s ENEM ([Nunes et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Pires et al.,
2023](#bib.bib34); [Santos and Campelo, 2023](#bib.bib39))—a national
multidisciplinary high-school-level exam widely used as an admission
test in Brazilian universities—and ENADE ([Almeida et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)). We briefly discuss these studies below to provide a
comprehensive backdrop against which the contributions of our work can
be contextualized and compared.

### 2.1. LLMs Evaluation in Logical Reasoning

[Bubeck et al. (2023)](#bib.bib6) showed that GPT-4 exhibited
significant logical reasoning capabilities in various domains, including
professional and academic benchmarks, where it performs at the human
level. The study also highlighted the model’s struggles with planning
and creative problem-solving due to its reliance on a sequential
prediction paradigm. Similarly, [Liu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib22) focused
on logical reasoning in reading comprehension and natural language
inference, finding that despite strong performances on known datasets,
GPT-4’s effectiveness diminishes with new, out-of-distribution data.
This observation points to a crucial gap in GPT-4’s capacity to handle
unfamiliar data types and logical inferences beyond its training data.
[Mao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib25) provided a more holistic view by
surveying assessments across various capabilities of ChatGPT and GPT-4,
indicating strong language understanding and generation skills but also
limitations in tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and domain-specific
knowledge. Finally, [Espejel et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9) compared
reasoning abilities across LLMs including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and BARD,
finding that while GPT-4 generally outperforms its predecessors and
competitors, all models show limitations in inductive, mathematical, and
multi-step reasoning tasks.

Building on these foundational studies, our study further explores the
capabilities of ChatGPT-4 Vision by evaluating its performance on the
ENADE 2021 BCS exam, which includes complex reasoning tasks in a
multimodal context. This extends the current understanding of LLMs’
capabilities by testing them on more challenging, real-world academic
assessments.

### 2.2. LLMs Evaluation in Computer Science Assessments

[Joshi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib17) evaluated the performance of
ChatGPT-3.5 across a variety of computer science exercises, including
true/false, multiple-choice, short and long answers, and coding-related
questions. The study demonstrated ChatGPT-3.5’s inconsistent accuracy
across subjects and question types, particularly in numerical-based
problems. Similarly, [Richards et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38) provide an
in-depth analysis of ChatGPT-3.5’s performance in a university computer
science curriculum. The study involved a blind marking exercise in which
the ChatGPT-generated answers were directly compared with those of human
students. The findings showed that barring two outliers, every
ChatGPT-3.5 answer achieved at least a passing grade. The study also
highlights that while ChatGPT-3.5 is capable of producing adequate
solutions in most cases, its performance varies across subjects and
question types, with ChatGPT-3.5’s effectiveness diminishing as the
complexity of the questions increases. [Jalil et al. (2023)](#bib.bib16)
explored ChatGPT-3.5’s performance in answering 31 questions from a
popular software testing textbook. The study found that ChatGPT-3.5
provided correct or partially correct answers and explanations for over
half of the questions tested, showcasing the model’s potential as an
educational tool. However, the study also noted ChatGPT’s inconsistent
accuracy and poor self-assessment, especially in questions that involved
both coding and conceptual understanding. [Bordt and von Luxburg
(2023)](#bib.bib5) investigated ChatGPT-3.5 and 4’s performance in an
undergraduate computer science exam focusing on algorithms and data
structures. ChatGPT-3.5 narrowly passed the exam with 20.5 out of 40
points, a result that was slightly below the performance of the average
student. ChatGPT-4 scored about 17% higher, reaching the average
student’s level. The study underlined the model’s challenges with
exercises requiring a detailed understanding of algorithmic processes,
particularly involving structured output that was not in pseudo-code
format. Finally, [Mahon et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23) investigated the
capabilities of ChatGPT-4 (no vision) on the UK A-Level and Irish
Leaving Certificate computer science examinations. They found that
ChatGPT-4 achieved high marks on both exams but struggled with questions
involving symbols or images and cascading questions where initial
inaccuracies led to further errors. This work underscores the strengths
and weaknesses of generative AI in educational assessments and has
implications for exam design and marking schemes.

Our research builds on these findings by not only evaluating ChatGPT-4
Vision on a comprehensive academic assessment in Computer Science but
also examining its performance relative to question difficulty and
discrimination levels. This provides a more nuanced understanding of the
model’s capabilities and limitations compared to the human participants,
which is extremely important in educational contexts.

### 2.3. LLMs Evaluation in Other Education Domains

[Nori et al. (2023)](#bib.bib28) presents a comprehensive evaluation of
ChatGPT-4’s performance on the United States Medical Licensing
Examination (USMLE) and the MultiMedQA medical benchmark. The study
found that GPT-4, without any specialized prompt crafting, surpassed the
passing score on the USMLE by over 20 points and outperformed previous
models like ChatGPT-3.5 and specialized medical models. The study also
explored ChatGPT-4’s calibration, crucial in high-stakes domains like
medicine, and found it to be significantly better than its predecessor.
Similarly, [Toyama et al. (2023)](#bib.bib40) investigated the
performance of ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and Bard on the official board
examination of the Japan Radiology Society. The study found that
ChatGPT-4 significantly outperformed ChatGPT-3.5 and Bard by over 20
percentage points, achieving an accuracy of 65% in the exam’s
multiple-choice questions. Both studies underscore the potential utility
of AI models in assisting professionals in high-stakes domains like
medicine, while also emphasizing the need for cautious application due
to the models’ limitations in accuracy and safety-critical tasks.

In the field of engineering, [Frenkel and Emara (2023)](#bib.bib11)
examined ChatGPT-3.5 and 4’s performance on the United States
Fundamentals of Engineering (FE) Mechanical Engineering Exam. The study
found that ChatGPT-4 significantly outperforms ChatGPT-3.5, achieving
76% correct answers compared to 51% by GPT-3.5. A similar study was
conducted by [Pursnani et al. (2023)](#bib.bib35) where they evaluated
GPT-3.5-Legacy, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and GPT-4’s performance across different
sections of the FE Environmental Exam. The study also found that GPT-4
outperformed GPT-3.5-Legacy and GPT-3.5-Turbo by a significant margin,
achieving 75% accuracy with slightly refined prompts. However, both
studies confirmed previous findings about ChatGPT’s error types and
pitfalls, noting its inconsistency across question types and subjects
and its tendency to confidently produce incorrect answers.

Our study contributes to this body of work by evaluating ChatGPT-4
Vision’s performance on a high-stakes academic exam (ENADE), involving
both textual and visual content. By allowing the model to reassess its
responses with differing answer keys, we explore its self-reflective
capabilities, a novel aspect not covered in previous education-centered
studies.

### 2.4. Recent Advances in VLMs

[Zhang et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib49) conducted a comprehensive evaluation
of state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4 Vision, on tasks requiring
visual deductive reasoning using Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPMs).
Their findings revealed significant challenges in models’ abilities to
perform multi-hop relational and deductive reasoning based solely on
visual cues, highlighting perception issues and difficulties in
understanding abstract patterns. [Mayne (2024)](#bib.bib26) proposed
improvements to GPT-4 Vision’s performance on visual reasoning tasks
through enhanced prompt engineering techniques. By incorporating
specific instructions in prompts, such as paying attention to details
and describing items with positional specificity, Mayne demonstrated
substantial improvements in the model’s accuracy on visual puzzles. [Wu
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib44) introduced the Visualization-of-Thought
prompting technique, which aims to elicit spatial reasoning in LLMs by
visualizing their reasoning traces. This technique enhances spatial
reasoning tasks, such as natural language navigation, visual navigation,
and visual tiling, by guiding subsequent reasoning steps through mental
image visualization. Finally, [Zhang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib48)
presented MathVerse, a specialized benchmark designed to evaluate the
visual mathematical reasoning skills of Multi-modal Large Language
Models (MLLMs). MathVerse includes a diverse set of 2,612 visual math
problems across three primary areas: plane geometry, solid geometry, and
functions. The study found that most existing MLLMs struggle to
understand math diagrams and often rely more on textual questions than
visual inputs, emphasizing the need for better visual encoding
capabilities.

Our work differs from these related studies in several ways but also
stands to benefit significantly from their insights and methodologies.
While [Zhang et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib49) provide a comprehensive
evaluation of VLMs on visual deductive reasoning tasks, our focus is on
assessing ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance in the context of the ENADE
exam, which involves a broader range of multimodal reasoning tasks
beyond visual deductive reasoning. The visual-enhanced prompt
engineering techniques proposed by [Mayne (2024)](#bib.bib26) and [Wu
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib44) could be particularly beneficial in improving
ChatGPT-4 Vision’s handling of spatial reasoning tasks within the ENADE
exam, guiding the model through intermediate steps via mental image
visualization. Furthermore, our work could benefit from the development
of a MathVerse-like fine-grained multimodal benchmark based on ENADE
questions with visual content to better evaluate and understand
ChatGPT-4 Vision’s capabilities in real-world educational assessments.

### 2.5. LLMs Evaluation in Brazil’s ENEM and ENADE

[Nunes et al. (2023)](#bib.bib29) studied GPT-3.5 and GPT-4’s
performance on answering multiple-choice ENEM questions, using different
prompt strategies, including Chain-of-Thought (CoT). GPT-4, especially
with CoT, achieved up to 87% accuracy on the 2022 exam, significantly
outperforming GPT-3.5. [Pires et al. (2023)](#bib.bib34) also examined
the performance of ChatGPT-3.5 and 4, the latter with and without Vision
capabilities, on the 2022 and 2023 editions of ENEM. The study showed a
clear advancement in performance from ChatGPT-3.5 to ChatGPT-4, with
GPT-4 models significantly outperforming their predecessors.
Specifically, ChatGPT-4 (no Vision) and ChatGPT-4 Vision achieved
accuracies of about 73% and 79% in the 2022 exam, and 80% and 86% in the
2023 exam, respectively. Interestingly, when provided with
human-generated captions transcribing the questions’ visual content,
ChatGPT-4 with no Vision capabilities improved its accuracies to 81% and
91% in the 2022 and 2023 exams, respectively, outperforming ChatGPT-4
Vision with images and no captions. [Santos and Campelo
(2023)](#bib.bib39) investigated the performance of quantized
open-source LLaMA-based models on a custom-built benchmark containing
over one thousand ENEM questions, showing that the best models achieved
an accuracy of 46% for the original texts of the Portuguese questions
and 49% on their English translations. Despite the modest computational
requirements of these open-source models, allowing them to run on
low-end hardware, their limited accuracy compared to that of closed
models indicates significant room for improvement. Finally, in a recent
study, [Almeida et al. (2024)](#bib.bib2) introduced Sabiá-2, a new
family of LLMs specifically trained on Portuguese texts and evaluated
its performance on a diverse range of exams, including a
multidisciplinary ENADE benchmark containing only multiple-choice
questions with no images from the 2022 and 2023 exams. The study
revealed that Sabiá-2, particularly the Sabiá-2 Medium model, matched or
surpassed GPT-4 Turbo’s performance in several ENADE disciplines and
significantly outperformed GPT-3.5 in all but one discipline. The
model’s lowest scores were achieved in domains related to engineering
and economics, with a particularly lower score compared to GPT-4 Turbo
in Computer Engineering.

Our work extends this area of research by evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision’s
performance on the ENADE BCS exam, which includes both open and
multiple-choice multimodal questions. Additionally, by involving an
independent panel of computer science researchers, we provide a more
rigorous assessment of the model’s accuracy and limitations in answering
ENADE questions, in addition to the questions’ overall quality.

## 3. Background

### 3.1. ENADE

Established in 2004 by the Brazilian Ministry of Education, the Exame
Nacional de Desempenho dos Estudantes (ENADE) is a federal government
exam that assesses the academic performance of undergraduate students in
Brazil, fostering an environment of continuous improvement in
educational standards ([Inep, 2023](#bib.bib15)). ENADE conducts annual
assessments targeting students who are nearing the completion of their
academic programs. The exam committee defines the knowledge areas to be
evaluated each year, with individual areas having their graduating
students assessed every three years.

The exam covers various disciplines—from computer science and
mathematics to history and philosophy—and encompasses bachelor,
teaching, and technology degrees. The exam consists of two primary
components: the first, the general education component, common across
various disciplines, assesses competencies and skills developed by
students and their general knowledge relating to Brazilian and global
realities. The second component, the specific knowledge component, is
tailored to each discipline, evaluating the mastery of knowledge and
skills expected for the discipline’s professional profile ([Inep,
2023](#bib.bib15)). Our study focuses on the specific knowledge
component of the ENADE 2021 BCS exam ([Inep, 2022](#bib.bib14)).

### 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam

ENADE’s BCS exam evaluates core computer science principles and concepts
such as algorithms, programming, operating systems, software
engineering, artificial intelligence, and distributed systems. At the
time of writing, the BCS exam had last been conducted in November 2021
with 10,119 participants from over 300 institutions across all five
regions of Brazil ([Inep, 2022](#bib.bib14)).

#### 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics

The 2021 BCS exam comprises three open questions and 27 multiple-choice
questions.
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
and
[2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
present the number, subject, modality (text or visual), and reasoning
strategy (requiring direct or indirect answers) for the open and
multiple-choice questions, respectively. Additionally,
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
lists the mean, median, and standard deviation scores (out of 100) for
the open questions.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
includes additional statistics for the multiple-choice questions, such
as the percentage of correct answers, facility level, point-biserial
correlation, and discrimination level. Two questions, 29 and 33
(highlighted in red in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")),
were invalidated after the exam, possibly due to poor construction. Note
that questions 01 and 02, as well as questions 06–08, are not listed in
these tables as they are general knowledge questions not related to
computer science.

The facility level classifies the percentage of correct answers for each
multiple-choice question into a hierarchy of levels, from Very Easy
($`\geq 0.86`$) to Very Hard ($`\leq 0.15`$), as outlined in
Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").
The discrimination level classifies the point-biserial correlation
([Bonett, 2020](#bib.bib4)) between participants’ performance on each
question and their overall performance in the exam into another
hierarchy of levels, from Very Good ($`\geq 0.40`$) to Weak
($`\leq 0.19`$), as shown in
Table [4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").
The point-biserial correlation is commonly used in academic exams to
measure the relationship between a student’s overall exam performance (a
continuous variable) and their response to a specific question (a
dichotomous variable, correct or incorrect) ([Rezigalla,
2022](#bib.bib37)). A higher point-biserial correlation for a question
indicates effective discrimination between students who score high
overall and those who score low. Questions with very low or negative
point-biserial correlation values may be seen as excessively difficult
or potentially flawed, as they do not align with the general performance
trends of the examinees and could be considered for exclusion from
scoring.

Table 5. ENADE 2021 BCS specific knowledge component scores.

ENADE 2021 calculates the final score of the specific knowledge
component by combining the scores of the open and multiple-choice
questions, with the former weighting 15% of the final score and the
latter weighting 85% ([Inep, 2022](#bib.bib14)). The open question score
is calculated as the average score of the three open questions. The
multiple-choice question score is calculated as the proportion of
correct responses to the remaining 19 out of the initial 27
multiple-choice questions. The final score is then converted to a scale
of 0 to 100, with 0 being the lowest possible score and 100 being the
highest.

Table [5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 3.2.2. Scores ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
presents the numbers for the open questions, multiple-choice questions,
and final scores for the 2021 BCS exam. The mean and median scores for
the open questions were 15.2 and 8.3, respectively, with a standard
deviation of 19.5. The mean and median scores for the multiple-choice
questions were 40.5 and 42.1, respectively, with a standard deviation of
16.5. Lastly, the mean and median scores for the final score were 36.7
and 35.8, respectively, with a standard deviation of 15.8. These numbers
indicate that the exam’s open questions were particularly challenging
for the participants. In contrast, the multiple-choice questions were
relatively more accessible, even though the average score in this
section was still below the 50% threshold. This result aligns with the
observation that nearly half of the 19 scored multiple-choice questions
were classified as Hard or Very Hard, as shown in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").

## 4. Study Method

Our study evaluates ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance on the specific
knowledge component of the ENADE 2021 BCS exam. To this end, we provided
the model with the exam’s questions in image format by taking a
high-resolution screen capture of each question’s page from the exam’s
official PDF document. Since the exam’s questions and response standard
are in Portuguese, we conducted the evaluation experiment in Portuguese,
including the model’s prompts and responses, and the expert assessments
of conflicting answers. We translated all materials into English for
this paper. Although we have not replicated the entire experiment using
the English translations of the questions, our experience with
ChatGPT-Vision and its successors is that these OpenAI models are as
good at answering questions in Portuguese as they are in English.

### 4.1. ChatGPT Versions Used in the Study

We used ChaGPT-4 Vision ([OpenAI, 2023c](#bib.bib32)) to answer ENADE’s
2021 BCS exam questions and ChatGPT-4 Turbo ([OpenAI,
2023d](#bib.bib33)), to reflect on ChaGPT-4 Vision’s performance on each
question. The reason we have not used ChatGPT-4 Turbo from the start is
that it was only released after we completed the question-answering
phase of the research using ChatGPT-4 Vision.

ChatGPT-4 Vision, released in September 2023, expands upon the
text-based capabilities of ChatGPT-4 by incorporating image analysis and
understanding ([OpenAI, 2023c](#bib.bib32)). It features a context
window of 32k tokens and an updated knowledge base until January 2022.
Since the ENADE 2021 exam was administered on November 14th, 2021, and
the exam key and response standard were made publicly available on March
18th, 2022, it is reasonable to assume ChatGPT-4 Vision’s knowledge base
did not include any information from the exam.

ChatGPT-4 Turbo, which was launched in November 2023, features a
significantly larger context window (128k tokens) compared to GPT-4,
allowing it to handle complex and lengthy prompts with greater accuracy
and coherence ([OpenAI, 2023d](#bib.bib33)). Additionally, ChatGPT-4
Turbo incorporates Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib20)), which integrates external information to enhance the
model’s responses. Furthermore, ChatGPT-4 Turbo boasts DALL-E 3
integration for text-to-image generation, text-to-speech capabilities
with multiple voice options, and an updated knowledge base extending to
April 2023.

### 4.2. Evaluation Procedure

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1. Question-answering evaluation procedure.

Our evaluation procedure for each exam question involved a multi-step
process, as illustrated in the activity diagram shown in
Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.2. Evaluation Procedure ‣ 4. Study Method ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").
Initially, we captured an image of the question from the exam’s PDF
file. We then provided this image along with a simple (zero-shot)
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib43)) to
ChatGPT-4 Vision, asking the model to answer the question depicted in
the image and to detail its reasoning step by step. This prompting
approach was chosen because it enables the model to demonstrate its
ability to understand and solve complex problems without prior specific
training on the exam’s content, relying instead on its general
pre-trained knowledge base. Moreover, by incorporating CoT prompts, the
evaluation process gains transparency and insight into the model’s
reasoning, allowing the assessment not just of the correctness of the
final answers but also of the logical processes used to arrive at them.
This is especially valuable in an educational context, where
understanding the steps of problem-solving is as important as the
solution itself.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
shows our study’s zero-shot CoT prompt templates for the ENADE 2021 BCS
open and multiple-choice exam questions.

After providing ChatGPT-4 Vision with the appropriate prompt, we
compared the model’s generated response against the exam’s official
answer standard (for open questions) or answer key (for multiple-choice
questions). When the model’s response did not align with the official
answer, we prompted the model to reassess its response in light of the
official answer and self-reflect on its possible reasoning mistakes.
Essentially, our reassessment prompts inform the model that its initial
answer is inconsistent with the official answer and instruct it to
ponder whether to maintain or change its initial answer given the new
information.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
shows our reassessment prompt templates for open and multiple-choice
questions. We interactively analyzed the model’s subsequent responses
and prompted it for further clarification when the model’s decision on
the correct answer was unclear or incoherent.

Following the clarification stage, if discrepancies persisted between
ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses and the official answer, the conflicting
answers were escalated to an independent expert panel for review. The
panel comprised two or more computer science researchers from multiple
Brazilian universities with known expertise on the question’s subject.
We provided each panel member with the question, official answer, and
ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses. They were individually asked to assess the
correctness of the model’s responses and provide their reasoning for
their decisions without knowing the identity and opinions of their
peers. The panel members were also asked to indicate if the question was
unclear or had multiple or no possible correct answers. We then compiled
and classified the panel’s assessments as conclusive or inconclusive.
Conclusive assessments were those where all panel members agreed on the
question’s correct answer. Inconclusive assessments were those where the
panel members disagreed on the correctness of the question’s answer or
indicated that the question was unclear or had no possible answer.

In the final evaluation step, we provided ChatGPT-4 Turbo with the
question image, ChatGPT-4 Vision’s prompts and responses, and the expert
assessments (when available) for each question in which the model did
not initially agree with the official response and prompted it to
reflect on the entire question-answering process. In particular, we
asked the model to identify the possible challenges the AI faced in
answering the question, the cause of its errors, and whether these
errors could be mitigated by using more sophisticated prompt engineering
techniques or would be inherent to the limitations of current LLMs. This
final reflective assessment aimed to provide further insights into the
AI’s reasoning and decision-making processes, contributing to a deeper
understanding of the model’s multimodal capabilities and limitations.

### 4.3. Question Scoring

We scored ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses to the three open questions using
the exam’s official answer standard as a reference. We assigned scores
from 0 to 100 to each response, where 0 indicated an utterly incorrect
response, and 100 indicated an entirely correct response. We scored
partially correct responses proportionally, based on the number of
correct items or assertions they contained. For example, a response with
two correct assertions out of three would be scored 66.6.

We scored ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses to the multiple-choice questions
proportionally to the number of responses that agreed with the exam’s
answer key. For reference, we scored all 25 valid multiple-choice
questions, including the six questions the exam committee excluded from
the final score. However, we only consider the 19 valid non-excluded
questions for computing the model’s final score.

We only scored the model’s initial response to each question and ignored
its subsequent reassessments or the expert panel’s reviews in
determining the score value. For example, if the model initially
answered a question incorrectly but later changed its response after
reassessment, we only considered the initial incorrect response for
scoring purposes.

### 4.4. Experimental Setup

During the question-answering sessions, we manually interacted with both
ChatGPT-4 Vision and ChatGPT-4 Turbo using their respective web
interfaces. We did not use an automated script for this task because
ChatGPT-4 Vision’s model was not available via API at the time the
experiment was conducted. We used the models’ default settings with no
parameter fine-tuning. We saved all the model’s prompts and responses
and the expert assessments as text files in their original Portuguese
version. We translated them into English using the GPT-4 Turbo API via a
customized Python script with minor manual revisions and improvements.
We also translated the exam’s official answer standard for open
questions into English using the same script.

## 5. Results

We now present the results for each of the five research questions
outlined in
Section [1](#S1 "1. Introduction ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").
We first analyze ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance in answering the ENADE
2021 BCS exam questions, focusing on the open and multiple-choice
questions. We then examine the model’s response changes when confronted
with disagreeing official answers and compare its final score with the
exam participants. Finally, we discuss the main challenges ChatGPT-4
Vision faced in answering the exam questions and reflect on its
reasoning and decision-making processes.

ChatGPT-4 Vision’s overall score, considering all 19 scored questions,
was 68.4, with 13 correct answers, five incorrect answers, and one
conflicting answer where the experts disagreed on the correct answer.
The model answered correctly 75.0% of questions with visual elements and
63.6% of text-only questions. The model showed a similar scoring pattern
for questions requiring direct and indirect answers, with 75.0% and
63.6% correct answers, respectively. These results indicate that the
model performed slightly better in questions with visual elements and
direct answers than in text-only questions or those requiring multi-step
answers.

The model’s performance degraded as the questions’ facility level
increased from Easy to Very Hard, with 100.0%, 75.0%, 62.5%, and 0.0%
correct answers, respectively. We observed a similar degradation pattern
in the model’s performance when grouping questions by discrimination
level, where it answered correctly 100.0%, 71.4%, and 42.9% of questions
classified as Very Good, Good, and Medium, respectively.

The model’s performance in the six excluded questions was significantly
lower than in the scored questions, with only 33.3% correct answers
compared to 68.4% in the first category. Even when grouping the excluded
questions by modality, reasoning strategy, and facility and
discrimination levels, the model did not get more than half of the
questions correct in either group. These results suggest that ChatGPT-4
Vision’s performance in the multiple-choice questions is generally
aligned with the overall performance of the exam’s participants, with
the model scoring higher in questions classified as Medium to Easy at
the facility level and Medium to Very Good at the discrimination level.

We applied Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient ([Zar,
2005](#bib.bib46)) to test this hypothesis by calculating the
correlation between the AI model’s performance and each question’s
facility and discrimination levels. This method was chosen for its
robustness in handling non-parametric data and its effectiveness in
measuring the strength and direction of association between two ranked
variables. The AI model’s answers were numerically coded to facilitate
the analysis: correct answers as 1 and 0 otherwise. The facility level
and the discrimination level were numerically represented by the
percentage of correct answers and the Point-Biserial correlation values,
respectively.

Our Spearman’s rank correlation analysis indicated a coefficient of
0.555 ($`p=0.004`$) between the AI model’s performance and the facility
level. The analysis also yielded a Spearman’s correlation coefficient of
0.584 ($`p=0.0022`$) when comparing the AI model’s performance with the
Point-Biserial Correlation values. These results reveal statistically
significant positive correlations ($`p<0.05`$) between the AI model’s
performance and the exam questions’ facility and discrimination levels,
as evidenced by the $`p`$-values reported. Thus, the correlation results
support our claim that ChatpGPT-4 Vision is more adept at answering
questions that are both easier for students and more discriminative
regarding student performance.

Table 8. ChatGPT-4 Vision’s responses and expert panel assessments for
multiple-choice questions with initially disagreeing responses.
Questions excluded from the final score due to a weak point-biserial
correlation are highlighted in light yellow. Questions where the expert
panel disagreed on the correct answer are highlighted in boldface.

Table [8](#S5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 5.3. RQ3: Performance in Questions with Disagreeing Answers ‣ 5. Results ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
shows ChatGPT-4 Vision’s initial and revised responses and the expert
panel’s assessments (when available) for the ten multiple-choice
questions where the model initially disagreed with the official answer.
This table reveals that the model initially disagreed and subsequently
agreed with the official answer key after reassessment in four questions
(12, 21, 26, and 34). These four questions were classified as Hard (21)
or Very Hard (12, 26, and 34), with two (12 and 21) being excluded from
the final score due to a Weak discrimination level (see
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")).
Notably, for questions 21 and 34, ChatGPT-4 Vision initially suggested
invalidation but revised its stance to align with the official answer
upon reassessment.

Out of the six questions where the model’s disagreement with the answer
key persisted after reassessment, the expert panel unanimously agreed
with the answer key in three questions (09, 14, and 31) and did not
agree on the correct answer for the remaining three questions (13, 18,
25). The three questions where the expert panel agreed on the correct
answer were classified from Medium (09) to Hard (14 and 31) at the
facility level and from Medium (09 and 14) to Good (31) at the
discrimination level. On the other hand, two of the three questions
where the expert panel disagreed on the correct answer (13 and 25) were
classified as Hard with a Weak discrimination level, thus being among
the six excluded from the final score. Question 18 is the exception from
this group since it was classified as Medium at the facility level and
Good at the discrimination level. This discrepancy means that the AI
model and the expert panel struggled to provide a definitive answer to a
question that a significant fraction of the exam’s participants did not
find particularly difficult.

The results in
Table [8](#S5.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 5.3. RQ3: Performance in Questions with Disagreeing Answers ‣ 5. Results ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
also reinforce the claim that the model’s performance tends to reflect
that of the human participants in the multiple-choice section of the
exam, with both the model and the expert panel struggling to provide a
definitive answer to some questions classified as Hard or Very Hard with
a Weak discrimination level.

### 5.5. RQ5: Challenges in Answering Open and Multiple-Choice Questions

[TABLE]

Table 10. Challenges ChatGPT-4 Vision faced in answering ENADE 2021 BCS
questions.

Based on our analysis of ChatGPT-4 Vision’s initially incorrect
responses, the expert assessments (when available), and ChatGPT-4
Turbo’s responses, we identified three challenges categories: Question
Interpretation, Logical Reasoning, and Visual Acuity. We further
classified the most common errors generated by the model when facing
each of these challenges into eight error types, as described and
illustrated in
Table [10](#S5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 5.5. RQ5: Challenges in Answering Open and Multiple-Choice Questions ‣ 5. Results ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam").
Question interpretation errors are caused by the model’s inability to
correctly interpret the questions’ statements. Logical reasoning errors
arise from the model’s flawed reasoning processes when answering the
assertions in the questions. Finally, visual acuity errors are caused by
the model’s inability to correctly identify and process the questions’
visual elements. These challenge categories and error types are not
mutually exclusive, as the manifestation of errors related to one
challenge may lead to the manifestation of other errors related to
another challenge. For example, the model’s misidentification of a
visual element in a question may trickle down to an incorrect multi-step
reasoning process.

The last column of
Table [10](#S5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 5.5. RQ5: Challenges in Answering Open and Multiple-Choice Questions ‣ 5. Results ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
reveals that the most common error types generated by ChatGPT-4 Vision
in answering the ENADE 2021 BCS questions were related to logical
reasoning, particularly incorrect multi-step reasoning (in five
questions), insufficient domain knowledge (in four questions), and
evaluation leniency (in three questions). Inconsistent responses and
misidentification of visual elements (in three questions each) were also
common error types. Other less frequent error types included incorrect
algorithmic reasoning and non-compliance with guidelines (in two
questions), and lack of domain-specific visual output (in one question).
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B ChatGPT-4’s Full Conversations and Experts’ Assessments ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")
shows the model’s conversations for the three open and six
multiple-choice questions illustrating most of these challenges
categories and error types. The model’s full conversations for all the
questions are available in the paper’s companion repository.

These results provide several insights into ChatGPT-4 Vision’s
multimodal reasoning capabilities. For example, the model’s frequent
incorrect multi-step reasoning and insufficient domain knowledge suggest
its ability to reason about complex, multi-step problems in computer
science is still limited. Moreover, the model’s multiple evaluation
leniency issues indicate its ability to evaluate the validity of
assertions is not yet as strict as that of the human experts. Finally,
the model’s tendency to misidentify visual elements and lack of
domain-specific visual output show that its visual acuity is not yet as
developed as its text-based reasoning capabilities. This limitation is
particularly critical given the frequent use of visual data in academic
assessments in computer science and other science and engineering
fields.

Another relevant result was the model’s struggle with vague or ambiguous
statements, particularly in questions where the expert panel did not
agree on the correct answer, such as in questions 13, 18, and 25. This
result suggests that some of the exam’s questions may have been poorly
constructed, leading to confusion and disagreement among the model and
the human experts. Indeed, some experts explicitly mentioned the low
quality of some ENADE questions, with one expert being even more
forthright when assessing the quality of one particular question: “I’m
sad that such a poorly formulated question was used to evaluate computer
science students.”

It is worth noting that these challenges did not manifest uniformly
across the open and multiple-choice questions. For example, the model’s
issues with incorrect multi-step reasoning were more frequent in the
multiple-choice questions with indirect answers. At the same time, the
lack of domain-specific visual output is only an issue for open
questions requiring visual responses. Moreover, some challenges were not
uniformly distributed across questions with similar characteristics. For
example, the model’s issues with misidentifying visual elements did not
occur in all questions containing figures or diagrams. These results
suggest that the model’s challenges are highly context-dependent and may
require tailored solutions to address them effectively.

## 6. Discussion

Given the results presented in the previous section, we discuss the
implications of ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance in the ENADE 2021 BCS
exam and the insights gained from the model’s challenges in answering
the exam’s questions. We also discuss the limitations of our study and
future research directions.

### 6.1. Implications of ChatGPT-4 Vision’s Performance

The performance of ChatGPT-4 Vision on the ENADE 2021 BCS exam
highlights significant advancements in AI’s ability to engage with
complex, multimodal academic content. The AI’s overall score, comparable
to that of the top-scoring human participants, particularly its superior
performance in open questions and its competitive edge in
multiple-choice questions with visual elements, underscores the
potential of multimodal AI in educational settings. These results
indicate the evolving capabilities of AI systems to process and analyze
information in a manner previously thought to be exclusive to human
cognition ([Zhai et al., 2024](#bib.bib47)). Such capabilities could be
harnessed to support various educational tasks, such as developing
advanced tutoring systems, aiding educational assessment, and providing
personalized learning experiences ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)). The
model’s ability to reason about complex, multimodal problems in computer
science is particularly promising, given the growing demand for AI
systems that can understand and reason about multimodal data in this
education domain ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib52)).

### 6.2. Insights from ChatGPT-4 Vision’s Challenges

The challenges faced by ChatGPT-4 Vision, particularly in logical
reasoning, question interpretation, and visual acuity, provide valuable
insights into the current limitations of AI in fully understanding and
responding to complex multimodal academic problems. The model’s
difficulties with incorrect multi-step reasoning and insufficient domain
knowledge reinforce similar findings reported by prior studies (e.g.,
([Bubeck et al., 2023](#bib.bib6); [Mao et al., 2023](#bib.bib24);
[Espejel et al., 2023](#bib.bib9))). Nevertheless, these insights
provide valuable guidance for future improvements to the model’s
reasoning capabilities, perhaps through more sophisticated training
datasets or advanced reasoning algorithms ([Tyen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib41)). The model’s challenges with visual acuity also
highlight the importance of developing AI systems that can accurately
interpret and integrate multi-modal inputs ([Zhao et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib50)). Furthermore, the model and expert panel’s struggle
with vague or ambiguous statements could inform educational assessment
design, helping improve the clarity and precision of questions during
exam elaboration. Finally, the finding that the model’s performance is
correlated with the difficulty and discriminative power of the exam’s
multiple-choice questions suggests that ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance
could be used as a proxy for question quality and complexity, thus
providing a valuable tool for exam creators to test and refine their
questions before administering the exam.

### 6.3. Study Limitations and Future Directions

Our study has certain limitations that are important to acknowledge.
First, the reliance on zero-shot CoT prompts may have limited the AI’s
ability to fully engage with the multi-step reasoning required by some
exam questions, potentially underestimating its true reasoning
capabilities. Future studies should experiment with advanced prompting
techniques like Self-Consistency ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib42)),
Tree-of-Thoughts ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib45)), and
Visualization-of-Thought ([Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)), which may
enable the AI to navigate complex reasoning sequences more effectively,
potentially revealing deeper insights into its problem-solving
abilities. The fact that ChatGPT-4 Vision was able to reassess and
correct its initial response to several questions during our experiment
suggests that new prompting techniques tailored for the exam’s format
and style have the potential to further enhance the model’s accuracy.
Second, our evaluation protocol involved asking the AI model to answer
each question only once. This design choice limits our ability to
analyze the consistency of the AI’s performance or its variability in
responding to the same question across multiple attempts. A more
comprehensive evaluation could involve multiple attempts to answer each
question, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of the AI’s
performance and the potential for improvement over time ([Chen et al.,
2023](#bib.bib7)). Third, our study did not compare ChaGPT-4 Vision’s
ENADE 2021 BCS exam performance with other multimodal generative AI
models like Google’s recently released Gemini family of models ([Gemini
Team, 2023](#bib.bib12)). A systematic comparative analysis involving
other multimodal generative AI models could provide valuable insights
into the unique capabilities and limitations of each model in handling
educational content. This approach could also help identify areas for
cross-model improvements and innovations ([Qi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib36)). Finally, our study did not incorporate traditional
exam validation methods, such as pre-assessment moderation, where human
experts review and validate exam questions to ensure their quality,
fairness, and alignment with educational objectives ([Bloxham et al.,
2016](#bib.bib3)). Incorporating such traditional methods could provide
a valuable benchmark against which the AI’s performance can be measured.
Future research could explore this comparison to better understand the
potential and limitations of AI in educational assessments.

## 7. Conclusion

ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance on Brazil’s ENADE 2021 Bachelor in
Computer Science exam offers a compelling glimpse into the future of
generative AI technologies in educational assessment. ChatGPT-4 Vision
not only matched but, in some cases, exceeded the top human scores,
particularly in handling questions with visual components and complex
problem-solving scenarios. While showcasing the model’s impressive
multimodal reasoning capabilities, the results particularly underline
the need for improvements in the AI’s handling of complex visual data
interpretations and its ability to apply domain-specific knowledge
accurately. Future research should focus on refining multimodal
generative AI models to enhance their interpretive, reasoning, and
vision capabilities. This includes exploring adaptive prompt techniques
that dynamically adjust based on the AI’s response quality, aiming to
steer AI models more effectively through complex reasoning pathways.
Additionally, employing AI models in simulated testing environments can
help identify biases, ambiguities, or inconsistencies in exam questions,
thereby enhancing their fairness and effectiveness. Successfully
addressing these challenges will not only advance AI’s capabilities in
educational assessments but also pave the way for broader applications
in personalized learning, automated tutoring systems, and interactive
educational content.

## Appendix A Prompt Templates

The following are the prompt templates used to guide ChatGPT-4 Vision
and ChatGPT-4 Turbo’s responses during the ENADE 2021 BCS
question-answering session. The templates are organized into three
categories: initial prompts, reassessment prompts, and reflective
prompts. Initial prompts are used to guide the model’s first response to
each question. Reassessment prompts are used to guide the model’s
self-reflective response when presented with a differing response
standard or answer key. Finally, reflective prompts are used to guide
ChatGPT-4 Turbo’s analysis of ChatGPT-4 Vision’s main challenges and
difficulties in answering the questions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Note that the main difference between the initial prompts for the two
types of questions is that multiple-choice prompts explicitly request
the model to select the correct answer from the five given alternatives.
In both cases, the prompts ask the model to explain its reasoning and
inform if the question is unclear or has multiple or no possible correct
answers.

## Appendix B ChatGPT-4’s Full Conversations and Experts’ Assessments

The following are ChatGPT-4’s full conversations and the human experts’
assessments—when available—for the three open questions and a
representative sample of six valid multiple-choice questions.

### B.1. Open Questions

#### [Question 03](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q03-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to analyze a truth table for a set of
formulas of propositional logic and answer four questions about the
formulas’ properties. ChatGPT-4 Vision gave correct answers to the first
and fourth questions, a partially correct answer to the second question,
and an incorrect answer to the third question. Upon being confronted
with the response standard for the question, the model admitted it did a
rush analysis of the truth table and confused the labels of some
columns. The model also failed to cross-validate information between the
formulas and the truth table, leading to the incorrect evaluation of one
of the formulas. This question shows the model’s understanding of
complex mathematical concepts such as propositional logic and its
limitations in correctly identifying and reasoning about structured
visual information such as tables.

#### [Question 04](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q04-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to describe the truth table and draw
the circuit diagram of a 1-bit full adder. ChatGPT-4 Vision correctly
built the truth table but failed to draw the circuit diagram. This
question highlights the model’s capacity to understand complex computer
architecture concepts such as logic circuits but also the model’s
current inability to generate domain-specific visual outputs such as a
circuit diagram.

#### [Question 05](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q05-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to answer questions regarding the
behavior and time complexity of a binary heap implementation in C whose
code is provided as part of the question. ChatGPT-4 Vision gave an
incorrect answer to the first question, where it failed to calculate the
final state of a given array after the execution of the binary heap
implementation with certain parameters, but correctly informed the
binary heap’s time complexity as the answer to the second question. This
question showcases the model’s capacity to understand complex
algorithmic concepts such as a sorting algorithm’s time complexity but
exposes the model’s limitations to correctly simulate the execution of a
piece of code in a step-by-step manner.

### B.2. Multiple-Choice Questions

#### [Question 11](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q11-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to identify the correct statements
regarding the improvement of a deep neural network architecture for a
specific image classification task and then select the alternative that
refers to those correct statements. ChatGPT-4 Vision accurately
identified the correct statements and their corresponding alternative
while providing a detailed explanation for its choice. This question
demonstrates the model’s capacity to understand complex multimodal
content in artificial intelligence and reason about it in a multi-step
process.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### [Question 13](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q13-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to select the correct statement
regarding iterative and evolutionary software development considering a
given reference text. ChatGPT-4 Vision chose a different alternative
from the answer key based on an inconsistent reasoning process where it
sometimes followed a strict interpretation of the question and sometimes
applied implicit domain knowledge not directly mentioned in the
reference text. This question showcases the model’s capacity to
understand complex software development concepts but also its struggles
with questions requiring implicit knowledge or inferences beyond the
provided text. The fact that the three experts did not reach a consensus
on the correct answer or the validity of the question also highlights
the potential ambiguity of the question and the critical need for better
quality control in the exam elaboration. Note: this question was one of
the six questions excluded from the final score due to a Weak
discrimination level (see
Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1. Questions and Statistics ‣ 3.2. 2021 Bachelor in Computer Science Exam ‣ 3. Background ‣ Evaluating ChatGPT-4 Vision on Brazil’s National Undergraduate Computer Science Exam")).

#### [Question 22](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q22-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to select the most appropriate
relational schema to be generated from a given Entity-Relationship
Diagram (ERD). ChatGPT-4 Vision correctly selected the most appropriate
alternative as the answer to the question. This question shows the
model’s ability to understand complex system modeling concepts such as
entities and relationships from a purely visual representation and
reason about them based on external domain knowledge.

#### [Question 28](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q28-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to assess the validity of four
statements about a theoretical model of an instruction pipeline,
visually illustrated in two accompanying figures, and then select the
alternative that contains only valid statements. ChatGPT-4 Vision
accurately evaluated the four statements, providing detailed
explanations for each of them, and selected the correct alternative as
the answer to the question. This question demonstrates the model’s
ability to understand complex computer architecture concepts such as
pipeline stages and their interactions over time and reason about them
based on external domain knowledge.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### [Question 31](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q31-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to evaluate four statements about the
behavior of a given Turing machine diagram. ChatGPT-4 Vision made
several mistakes in attempting to evaluate these statements. First, the
model failed to exclude the “B” symbols from the tape content when
evaluating statements I and II, as instructed by the question. Second,
the model failed to correctly interpret some labels in the Turing
machine diagram, leading to an incorrect analysis of the machine’s
operations. Third, perhaps due to these previous two errors, the model
made an incorrect interpretation of the machine’s actions, especially
regarding the substitution and movement of the reading head, leading to
an erroneous conclusion about the content of the tape after the
requested number of moves. Upon being confronted with the answer key and
challenged with multiple clarification prompts, the model made several
revisions to its initial response but ultimately concluded that all four
statements were true and thus the question had no correct answer. The
full conversion with the model was then escalated to two human experts
who unanimously agreed that the answer key was correct. This question
shows that ChatGPT-4 Vision’s performance can significantly be affected
by its inability to correctly interpret key diagram labels and to
accurately simulate an abstract machine’s operations. Moreover, the
model tends to overlook its limitations due to its typical
overconfidence in question-answering tasks.

#### [Question 34](https://github.com/nabormendonca/gpt-4v-enade-cs-2021/blob/main/questions/q34-eng.md)

This question asks the respondent to apply Dijkstra’s shortest path
algorithm to a given directed graph and then determine the cost estimate
after two iterations of the algorithm starting from a given vertex.
ChatGPT-4 Vision initially misidentified some weights of the edges in
the provided graph, causing an erroneous calculation of the distances
between some nodes and ultimately leading the model to conclude that no
alternative was correct. After being challenged with the answer key and
multiple clarification prompts, the model re-evaluated the graph’s
labels, correctly identified the weights of interest, and finally agreed
with the answer key. This question demonstrates that ChatGPT-4 Vision
can accurately apply complex algorithms to solve graph-based problems
but may struggle to reach the correct solution on the first attempt due
to the potential misidentification of important visual data. Moreover,
the model’s typical overconfidence in its initial response indicates a
dependence on external stimuli to re-assess and ultimately change its
conclusions.
